text:
I am a naked soul in these verses,

a naked soul that, anguished and alone,

leaves its petals scattered.


A soul that may be a poppy,

that may be a lily, a violet,

a crag, a forest, and a wave.


A soul that, like the wind, wanders restless

and roars when it is over the seas,

and sleeps sweetly in a cleft.


A soul that adores upon its altars

gods who do not stoop to blind it;

a soul that knows no barriers.


A soul that would be easy to master

with just a heart that broke open

to water it with its warm blood.


A soul that, when spring arrives,

tells lingering winter: return,

let your snow fall upon the meadow.


A soul that, when it snows, dissolves

in sadness, crying out for the roses

with which spring wraps us.


A soul that at times releases butterflies

into the open country, without setting a distance,

and tells them: sip from all things.


A soul that must die of a fragrance,

of a sigh, of a verse in which one begs,

without, if it can, losing its elegance.


A soul that knows nothing and denies everything

and, denying what is good, brings about the good

because it is by denying that it gives itself most.


A soul that often finds delight

in touching souls, despising the trace,

and feeling a caress in its hand.


A soul always discontented with itself,

wandering, running, turning like the winds;

a soul that bleeds and raves without cease

to be the star's ship underway.

translation.title: Naked Soul
translation.editorial_note: The translation preserves the repeated “Alma que” anaphora and the poem’s shifting natural forms, allowing the Spanish rhyme to give way to clear English images.
